g.text: Test your knowledge of MRI scan interpretation, pulse sequence parameters, image contrast, and scanner physics.
Spin Echo | TR: 500 ms | TE: 12 ms | Plane: Axial Brain
Notice: Fluid in the cerebral ventricles is dark; cerebral white matter is brighter than gray matter.
What is the contrast weighting of this brain scan?
— Short TR and short TE produce bright fat/white matter and dark fluid.
— Long TR and long TE produce bright fluid.
— Long TR and short TE minimize both T1 and T2 effects.
— Measures random Brownian motion of water molecules.
Short TR (500 ms) limits longitudinal relaxation so tissues with fast recovery (fat/white matter) are bright, while short TE (12 ms) minimizes transverse decay
Scan Readout: Inversion Time (TI) = 2500 ms, TR = 9000 ms, TE = 100 ms
An MRI brain scan uses a long TR (9000 ms), long TE (100 ms), and an Inversion Time (TI) of 2500 ms. The ventricles (CSF)
appear dark, but lesions in the periventricular white matter appear bright. What sequence is this?
FLAIR uses an inversion pulse with an inversion time (TI) chosen to null the signal of free fluid (CSF). Because TR and TE are long, pathology
Scan Readout: b = 1000 s/mm² • Hyperintense region indicating restricted water diffusion.
This ultrafast sequence uses strong bipolar diffusion gradients to detect cytotoxic edema and acute stroke within minutes of
symptom onset. What imaging technique is shown?
Proton Density weighted Fast Spin Echo
DWI sensitizes the MRI signal to the microscopic Brownian motion of water molecules. In acute cellular ischemia, cellular swelling restricts water
Scan Readout: Repetitive ghosting patterns propagating across the image.
Notice the repeating ghost copies of the skull propagating across the phase encoding direction. What artifact is occurring and what
Chemical Shift Artifact caused by water-fat frequency difference
Motion / Ghosting Artifact caused by patient movement or arterial pulsation —
Aliasing (Wrap-around) caused by too small a field of view
Gibbs Truncation Ringing caused by low matrix resolution
Patient movement (blinking, swallowing, breathing, or vascular pulsation) introduces phase errors between successive phase-encoding steps,
projecting ghost artifacts along the phase-encoding axis.
